profiles.meeting_scenario: Two weeks before submitting the replication package and final appendix for an empirical software engineering paper, the study's research engineer and the lab's data platform engineer meet to coordinate a last pipeline rerun and the handoff of shared artifacts. The project analyzes GitHub Actions workflows, SECURITY policy files, and CodeQL usage across large cohorts of popular GitHub repositories. The agenda is to align on which repository cohorts will be rerun, what counts should populate the appendix tables, and what exactly should go into the public artifact bundle. The expected outcome is a seemingly straightforward agreement that Lucas will regenerate the data and send Priya the final dataset and supporting files for submission.

members.name: Priya Natarajan
members.expertise: Empirical software engineering, mining software repositories, reproducibility for research artifacts
members.background: Priya leads the analysis for the paper and wrote most of the scripts that compute the reported percentages and language-level breakdowns from cleaned repository cohorts.
members.private_state: She wants the final appendix numbers to remain consistent with the draft already circulated to coauthors and is anxious about introducing last-minute drift that would force table rewrites or methodological clarifications.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'top repositories,' it refers to the post-processed cohort after removing forks, mirrors, archived repositories, and duplicates across query sources.
A repository only 'has a security policy' if GitHub would recognize a SECURITY.md-style policy on the default branch at scan time.
The study cohort was effectively frozen when the draft tables were produced, so any final rerun should reuse that snapshot unless someone explicitly reopens the methodology.
For a paper artifact, the expected handoff is the cleaned analysis-ready table plus scripts and figure outputs, not the raw extracted file inventory.

members.name: Lucas Meyer
members.expertise: Repository crawling, ETL pipelines, GitHub API ingestion, dataset packaging
members.background: Lucas maintains the crawler and nightly mirror that fetch repository metadata, workflow files, and security-related documents used by several mining studies in the lab.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid one-off special cases in the pipeline and prefers to deliver a standard reproducibility bundle generated from the latest successful crawl with minimal manual intervention.
hidden_assumptions: When someone asks for the 'top repositories' dataset, they usually mean the raw ranked pulls produced by the query jobs unless exclusions are separately requested downstream.

A repository has 'a security policy in place' if contributors can find vulnerability-reporting instructions anywhere the crawler detects them, including README, CONTRIBUTING, or non-default-branch policy files.
Unless a snapshot freeze is called out explicitly in the ticket or meeting, the correct operational default is to regenerate from the newest complete mirror.
A normal artifact package should include raw extraction outputs such as file paths, commit SHAs, and parser manifests in addition to any cleaned summary tables.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to rerunning the analysis on the 'top repositories' and updating the 'top-repo dataset.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means the final eligible analysis cohort after deduplication and exclusions already applied for the paper's tables.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Lucas means the raw top-N repository pulls returned by the crawler before paper-specific filtering and cross-list deduplication.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have repeatedly used the phrase internally for months, and because filtered cohorts are derived from the raw pulls, surface agreement feels safe even though they are imagining different concrete objects.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as 'a security policy in place'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss updating the percentage of repositories that have 'a security policy in place.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya counts only repositories with a GitHub-recognizable SECURITY.md-style policy on the default branch at the time of scanning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Lucas counts any repository where the crawler found vulnerability-reporting guidance anywhere, including README or CONTRIBUTING text and policy files outside the default branch.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about the same high-level concept of vulnerability disclosure guidance, so the standard sounds shared even though their threshold for what qualifies is different.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to using 'the same snapshot' or doing a 'final rerun' for the submission package.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya assumes 'same snapshot' means the January frozen export used to generate the circulated draft tables, preserving reproducibility and avoiding drift.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Lucas assumes 'final rerun' means the newest complete nightly mirror, because freshness is the default unless a freeze is explicitly restated.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both think the snapshot choice was already settled outside the meeting, so each treats their own assumption as background context rather than something needing confirmation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Lucas will send the 'artifact package' or 'final dataset' for submission.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya expects an analysis-ready CSV of repository-level indicators, the final figures, and the scripts needed to reproduce the tables in the paper.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Lucas expects to send the standard full bundle: raw extracted workflow and security file inventories, parser outputs, commit SHAs, manifests, and the summary CSV.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see their version as the obvious content of an artifact handoff, and because one is a superset of the other, nothing in the conversation forces them to notice the mismatch.
